notes.meaning: God gave Jeremiah this message early in the reign of King Jehoiakim of Judah. Although this chapter is placed after chapter 25 in the book, it records events that happened earlier in time.

God told Jeremiah to stand in the outer courtyard of the temple, where people from across Judah gathered for the major religious festivals. He was ordered to deliver God's entire message without holding back or softening a single word.
God offered the people an opportunity to turn away from their wicked lives. If they repented and changed their ways, God promised to withhold the disaster he had planned to bring on them.

differ.view: God's eternal mind never changes; he speaks here in human terms to show that he treats people with mercy whenever they turn from sin.
God's warnings of judgment are conditional, meaning he consistently withholds punishment when people repent and brings judgment when they do not.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God does not literally change his mind, but uses conditional warnings in scripture while respecting human free will.

notes.meaning: God warned the people that they must walk in his law and listen to the prophets he had sent again and again. If they refused to obey, God would ruin the temple just as he had destroyed the ancient sanctuary at Shiloh centuries earlier. The ruined city of Jerusalem would then become a proverb of cursing throughout all nations.

A large crowd in the temple courts heard Jeremiah deliver this warning. This audience included the priests, rival prophets who falsely claimed to speak for God, and ordinary worshipers visiting from across the land.

As soon as Jeremiah finished preaching, the priests, prophets, and crowd seized him and shouted that he deserved to die. They accused him of blasphemy for saying the temple and city would be destroyed, wrongly believing that God's presence meant the temple could never fall.

When the royal officials in the king's palace heard the commotion, they came up to the temple to restore order. They sat down at the entrance of the New Gate, which served as a public place to conduct formal trials.
The priests and false prophets brought their charges before the judges and the people. They demanded the death penalty, arguing that preaching against the holy city was treason and false prophecy.
Jeremiah defended himself calmly before the rulers and the gathering. He did not take back a word, but declared that the Lord himself had sent him to speak everything they had heard.

Instead of begging for mercy, Jeremiah urged his hearers to repent and obey God's voice. He reminded them that his warning was not a final sentence of doom, but an opportunity to turn back so that God would spare them.

Jeremiah placed himself in the hands of the judges, submitting calmly to their authority. At the same time, he warned them that executing him would bring the heavy guilt of killing an innocent prophet on the rulers, the city, and its people.

The officials and the crowd were convinced by Jeremiah's honest defense and declared him not guilty. They refused to execute him because they recognized that he had truly spoken in the name of the Lord.
Respected elders from the land stood up before the whole assembly. They used their wisdom and long memory of the nation's past to support the court's decision to protect Jeremiah.

The elders recalled that the prophet Micah had announced the very same destruction of Jerusalem a century earlier during the reign of King Hezekiah. Instead of executing Micah, Hezekiah had feared the Lord and prayed, and God spared the city. The elders warned that killing Jeremiah would bring terrible harm on their own nation.
The account notes that another man named Uriah had also prophesied in the Lord's name. Uriah delivered the exact same warnings against Jerusalem and Judah that Jeremiah had proclaimed.
When King Jehoiakim and his royal officers heard Uriah's warnings, the king wanted him put to death. Uriah became afraid and fled across the border into Egypt to escape.

King Jehoiakim sent royal officers to Egypt, where they arrested Uriah and brought him back. The king killed Uriah with a sword and threw his body into a common public graveyard, denying him the honorable burial given to prophets.

Even though King Jehoiakim was executing prophets, a powerful leader named Ahikam stepped in to help Jeremiah. Ahikam used his high influence at court to shield Jeremiah so the mob could not put him to death.
